newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX traders cautious on lifting of Taiwan ban.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX traders cautious on lifting of Taiwan ban.

text.p: Taiwan's impending removal of a ban on local trading of Taiwan-linked offshore stock index futures is generating guarded optimism from traders on Singapore's futures exchange.

The lifting of the ban is expected to boost volumes for Taiwan stock index futures traded on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), but traders said on Wednesday they were not anticipating an immediate flood of new business.
"The feeling is quite mixed about whether the Taiwanese will participate in this market," said a bond manager at a Japanese merchant bank.
He said Taiwan investors currently accounted for less than a quarter of the daily turnover in Nikkei 225 stock index futures traded on SIMEX.
"Volumes might go up, but I don't think we're going to reach 10,000-20,000 lots so soon. If we see 5,000 lots daily, that would be quite good," he said.
He said Taiwanese participants might be discouraged from trading the SIMEX contracts due to foreign exchange risks and Taiwan's strict controls on capital flows.
Taiwan's Securities and Futures Commission said last month it would lift from August 1 a ban on trading of Taiwan stock index futures listed on SIMEX and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME).
Both contracts were launched on January 9 despite objections from Taiwan regulators lobbying for time to establish Taiwan's own futures market.
Taipei was previously expected to lift the ban in April and then in June but the move was repeatedly postponed.

The SIMEX contract, based on the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) index, has fared better than the CME's Dow Jones Taiwan Stock Index futures, with daily volumes averaging between 1,000 and 2,000 lots.
But dealers and analysts said the contract would need to generate daily turnover in the region of 5,000 lots to attract, and retain, institutional interest.
Perry Gilbert, vice president of Refco Singapore Pte Ltd, was upbeat about the contract's prospects once Taiwanese retail investors are able to trade it.
"I think daily volumes will easily double over the first month. We could even see it reach 10,000-15,000 lots, but it's hard to say," Gilbert said.

Other dealers said the expected establishment of Taiwan's futures exchange in October could dampen interest as Taiwan was then likely to launch a futures contract based on its own weighted share index.

"If they lift the ban, it'll help Singapore substantially. But looking at the other side of the coin, once they start their own contract in October, the business will go there," a trader at an Asian institution said.
